facts: The question that falls for determination in the instant case is about the ambit of the inherent powers of the High Court's under Section 482, Code of Criminal Procedure (Code) read with Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India to quash criminal proceedings.

The matrimonial disputes of the kind in the present case have been on considerable increase in recent times resulting in filing of complaints by the wife under Sections 498A and 406, IPC not only against the husband but his other family members also.
Their marriage had taken place on 21st July, 1999.
They are living separately since 15th July, 2000.
FIR No.8 of 2002 was registered under Section 498A/323 and 406 IPC at Police Station, Central Faridabad at the instance of the wife on 2nd January, 2002.
She has filed an affidavit that the FIR was registered at her instance due to temperamental differences and implied imputations.
According to that affidavit, her disputes with the appellants have been finally settled and she and Appellant No.4 have agreed for mutual divorce.
The affidavit further states that on filing of the petition for mutual divorce, statements on first motion were recorded on 18th July, 2002 and 2nd September, 2002.
Also that in second motion filed by the parties to the marriage, their statements were recorded by the Court of Additional District Judge, Delhi on 13th September, 2002.
issues: The ambit of the inherent powers of the High Court's under Section 482, Code of Criminal Procedure (Code) read with Articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution of India to quash criminal proceedings.

Whether the offences under Sections 498A and 406 IPC are non-compoundable and the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code cannot be invoked to bypass the mandatory provision of Section 320 of the Code.
petitioner_arguments: The appellants seeking quashing of the FIR for in view of the High Court the offences under Sections 498A and 406 IPC are non-compoundable and the inherent powers under Section 482 of the Code cannot be invoked to bypass the mandatory provision of Section 320 of the Code.
There is, however, serious opposition on behalf of the State.
respondent_arguments: The respondent supporting the appeal also prays for quashing of the FIR.
There is, however, serious opposition on behalf of the State.
court_reasoning: The High Court has lost sight of the earlier part which made it abundantly clear that the said categories of cases were being given by way of illustration.
It is well settled that these powers have no limits.
Exercise of such power would depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case but with the sole purpose to prevent abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice.
The decision in Madhu Limaye's case has been misread and misapplied by the High Court.

It is, thus, clear that Madhu Limaye's case does not lay down any general proposition limiting power of quashing the criminal proceedings or FIR or complaint as vested in Section 482 of the Code or extra ordinary power under Article 226 of the Constitution of India.
holding: The petition filed by the appellants seeking quashing of the FIR is allowed.
The FIR No.8 of 2002 registered under Section 498A/323 and 406 IPC at Police Station, Central Faridabad at the instance of the wife on 2nd January, 2002 is hereby quashed.
